extracted.intended_audience: humour researchers, folklorists, digital culture / media scholars, and postgraduate students studying internet memes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical, folkloristic analysis of visual internet humour (memes and virals), focusing on how they travel, are adapted, and become locally meaningful; includes dataset selection and categorisation procedures. Useful for designing or evaluating memetic/viral studies and for understanding criteria of memetic success and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes vs Virals distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent research stresses the importance of differentiating between memes and virals and seeing them as two ends of a dynamic spectrum. Virals are single cultural units spread and viewed by millions, whereas a meme is a collection of texts (Shifman 2014: 56–58).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction for classification: virals = distributed without modification; memes = modified/adapted before sharing and produce derivative variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of successful memes (Knobel & Lankshear 2005)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful memes include one or more of the following characteristics: (1) some element of humour (absurd, parodying, geeky, etc); (2) rich kind of intertextuality, such as wry cross-references to different popular culture events, icons, or phenomena; and/or (3) anomalous juxtapositions, usually of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating memes, check for humour type, degree of intertextual references, and presence of striking/novel juxtapositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality / reliance on cultural memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Intertextual references rely partly on the cultural memory of a particular community and partly on global cultural influences, producing hybrid cultural texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a meme invokes prior texts/icons and whether those references are accessible/meaningful to the target audience; stronger intertextuality often yields greater insight into local/global cultural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to modification / polysemy increases popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more interpretations are accessible for the audience (cf. polysemy), the more popular the text becomes, whereas the range of interpretations depends on the openness of the cultural item to further modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate memetic items by their affordance for reinterpretation and remix; items that are easily repurposed tend to spawn many derivatives and gain popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visuality promotes spread
rubrics_metrics.description: In online contexts, visuality might promote the spread of memes, making them more available for internet users as linguistic barriers are minimised in an image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the extent to which visual elements reduce language-dependence and enable cross-cultural dissemination; visual base often underpins global transmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images travel well; text needs adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the images that travel well in their original form, whereas the text (translated, original, or completely altered) needs more adjustment. Visual side usually makes the base of the meme, whereas the text adds new layers of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting memes, prioritize retaining salient visual templates and modify textual overlays to localise meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability / ubiquity of the source meme
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes chosen for modification should be readily available (the popular ones are more ubiquitous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and analysts should prefer widely-circulated base images/videos for remixing, because ubiquitous templates invite more participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity / low complexity preference
rubrics_metrics.description: They should not be too complicated; the most popular videos and photos are not the high quality ones. Rather the opposite is true: the low-fi shaky videos and blurry pictures prove to be accepted by the crowd as the most appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, low-fi formats lower barriers to remix and sharing; complexity can hinder spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human agency and tactical decisions in diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Human agency – the choice of forwarding/modifying/commenting on/liking etc. a meme or a viral – is essential in the diffusion of these items of digital culture. Memes/virals do not replicate themselves; their circulation is guided by tactical decisions of users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for sender intentions and social motivations rather than treating memetic spread as automatic replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic translatability (easy vs complex topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Better-travelled humorous items mostly dwell on general popular topics such as sex or animals; such topics translate easily. Politics, nations, or specific, locally known group stereotypes translate less easily and often require adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect 'easy topics' to circulate as unmodified virals; political or culturally-specific topics typically undergo localisation and remixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder-based vs remixed meme replicability (high-fidelity vs remixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typology differentiates between high fidelity static memes (replicated with little change) and remixed ones which are replicated via evolution, adaptation or transformation of the original meme vehicle (Knobel & Lankshear; Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify circulating items accordingly; founder-based memes may spawn fewer localised textual variants compared to remixed templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localisation patterns: resemiotisation and entextualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemiotisation: content lifted from a source domain and recast in a modified form during production of a derivative text. Entextualisation: rendering coherent stretches of discourse discontinuous with one’s surroundings via meaning-making, adjusting cultural texts to be meaningful in the target culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these processes to describe and evaluate how global memetic materials are transformed into locally meaningful items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of widely known images plus local textual references
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally originating memes often use a 'global model' to start off a local meme: pasting local verbal parts onto universal visual meme backgrounds; the opposite configuration (local visuals with English/Russian text) is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective localisation, combine globally-recognised image templates with locally-relevant textual or referential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual adaptation as success indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: When humour travels across borders and is adapted to the target culture while retaining a connection with the source, popularity indicates that the adaptation was successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge adaptation success by the degree to which the derivative retains recognisability of the source while adding locally resonant meaning and by measures of popularity/engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of popularity via combined engagement metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The study selected items based on a combined popularity rating: a combined number of likes, shares/forwards, and comments as the indicator; likes, shares, and comments were used as equals in the combined popularity rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling memetic datasets, consider combining multiple engagement signals, but acknowledge that motivations behind each signal vary and may need separate analysis later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset selection and sampling criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset compiled from (1) Estonian major humour websites and (2) browsing for Estonian users on global meme sites, social media (Facebook), and video sharing sites (YouTube). Sources selected according to popularity rating; Estonian users on international sites chosen by cumulative method following social networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sources using popularity indicators and cross-check via forum threads/discussion to validate observations; document selection heuristics and any scripts used (the authors used a python script to rank by combined popularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorisation procedure for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Final sample was categorised into two categories – virals and memes – by the authors. Categories were broken down into thematic sections (daily politics, animals, ethnic groups etc.). Qualitative data analysis tool QDA Miner was used for tagging texts/images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing memetic corpora, apply clear categorisation rules, use thematic tagging, and employ QDA or similar tools to quantify frequencies and enable qualitative inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of local cultural motifs and celebrity substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic replacement often uses local celebrities, scandalous politicians, or modified Soviet/Russian posters to create locally meaningful variants (e.g. replacing figures in a famous poster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether local substitutions increase recognition and engagement; tracking the lineage of visual templates helps map intertextual networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political content tends to be heavily remixed and to catalyse engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Political topics (e.g., the 2015 refugee crisis) provoked many local memetic responses, with high levels of intertextuality and engagement; political memes do more than just criticise — they involve people and can mix critical commentary with absurd meta-comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect political topics to generate dense intertextual webs and to require contextual knowledge for full interpretation; use thematic and contextual analysis to evaluate such memes.
